issues.legal_issue: The pre-constitutional requisition law and its later amendments remained constitutionally valid despite the absence of express public-purpose language in the original law and presidential assent to the amendments.
material_facts: The requisition law was enacted before the Constitution came into force and was an existing law at that time.
The original law did not expressly state that requisition must be for a public purpose, but its purpose could be gathered from its tenor and intendment.
A later amendment extended the law, and another amendment expressly required requisition for a State or other public purpose with retrospective effect.
The amendments did not receive the President’s assent.
The constitutional challenge relied on property rights and the requirements governing requisition and post-Constitution legislation.
issues.conclusion: The law was saved as an existing law, and the amendments were valid without presidential assent; the law did not contravene the relevant fundamental rights.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 31(2), 31(3), 31(5)(a), 31(6) and 13 of the Constitution were applied. Under State of Bombay v. Bhanji Munji, the law was not invalid merely because the original text lacked express public-purpose language where that purpose followed from the law’s tenor and intendment. The saving for existing laws in Article 31(5)(a) applied; Article 31(3), which concerns laws made after the Constitution commenced, did not apply to amendments that extended or made explicit the substantive existing law. Because the existing law was not inconsistent with Part III, the amendments were also valid.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_requisition_law and law_enacted_before_constitution and public_purpose_inferable_from_law and amendments_extend_or_clarify_existing_law

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_requisition_: A party challenges the constitutional validity of a law authorizing requisition.
predicates.law_enacted_before_constitution: The requisition law was enacted before the Constitution came into force.
predicates.public_purpose_inferable_from_law: The law’s overall tenor and intendment show that requisition serves a public purpose, even if its original text does not say so expressly.
predicates.amendments_extend_or_clarify_existing_la: Later amendments extend the existing law or make explicit a purpose already inferable from it.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a pre-constitutional requisition law whose public purpose is inferable and later amendments merely extend or clarify that law, the law and amendments remain valid.

issues.legal_issue: Statutory declarations that a tenant had not resided in premises for the specified period or that premises had become vacant were conclusive and could not be reopened as factual findings in constitutional review.
material_facts: The requisition order declared that the premises had become vacant at the stated time.
The law made the Government’s declarations about the tenant’s residence and the premises’ vacancy conclusive evidence.
The petitioner sought to contest the factual basis for those declarations in constitutional proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The courts could determine whether the statute had been complied with, but could not reopen the Government’s conclusive findings about residence or vacancy.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 5 and 6 of the Bombay Land Requisition Act made the specified declarations conclusive evidence. Articles 32 and 226 preserve judicial power to determine whether statutory requirements were complied with, but do not permit reopening findings that the statute makes conclusive. Rai Brij Raj Krishna v. S. K. Shaw & Brothers was applied to support the rule that a statutory decision-maker’s determination on an entrusted issue may not be challenged merely because it was allegedly wrong; Hubli Electricity Co. Ltd. v. Province of Bombay was distinguished because the statute considered there did not make the relevant matters conclusive evidence.

predicates.constitutional_writ_review_of_requisitio: A party seeks constitutional review of a requisition decision.
predicates.statute_makes_residence_or_vacancy_findi: The governing law expressly makes the decision-maker’s finding about residence or vacancy conclusive evidence.
predicates.challenge_targets_that_finding: The challenger asks the court to reconsider the factual finding about residence or vacancy.

issues.definition: In constitutional review of a requisition, a conclusive statutory finding about residence or vacancy cannot be reopened when that finding is the object of the challenge.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s cessation of occupation for a reason outside the listed examples could constitute vacancy under the statutory phrase ‘or otherwise’.
material_facts: The Government found that the tenant had ceased occupying the premises and had handed possession to another occupant.
The petitioner argued that vacancy could arise only through termination of tenancy, eviction, assignment or transfer, and that the tenant’s circumstances did not fit those examples.
The statutory definition used the words ‘or otherwise’ after listing particular ways occupation could cease.
issues.conclusion: The words ‘or otherwise’ were words of extension covering all possible causes of vacancy, not words limited to causes of the same kind as the listed examples.
issues.legal_principle: Explanation (a) to section 6 of the Bombay Land Requisition Act treated premises as vacant when the relevant occupier ceased occupation upon termination, eviction, assignment or transfer, ‘or otherwise’. The rule of ejusdem generis applies to general words following specific words only where the context and statutory scheme support a restricted meaning. The Court applied the ordinary, inclusive meaning of the catchall phrase, relying by illustration on Skinner & Co. v. Shew & Co.

rule.if: vacancy_based_requisition_proceeding and occupier_ceased_occupying and vacancy_definition_uses_unqualified_catchall and cessation_reason_outside_listed_examples

predicates.vacancy_based_requisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns requisition based on a finding that premises are vacant.
predicates.occupier_ceased_occupying: The tenant or other relevant occupier stopped occupying the premises.
predicates.vacancy_definition_uses_unqualified_catc: The governing definition follows listed causes of vacancy with general catchall words.
predicates.cessation_reason_outside_listed_examples: The reason occupation ceased does not fall within the specifically listed causes.

issues.definition: When a relevant occupier ceases occupation for a reason outside the listed examples, an unqualified catchall in the vacancy definition allows that reason to constitute vacancy.

issues.legal_issue: An administrative requisition order did not become ineffective merely because a person named in it had died before it was made.
material_facts: The requisition order named the deceased former tenant among the persons to be served, although he had died before the order was made.
The order was an administrative requisition order, not an order in judicial proceedings between the Government and the named persons.
The petitioner learned of the order when a copy was affixed to the premises.
The law provided for service of orders and stated that failure to comply with its service requirements did not affect an order’s validity.
issues.conclusion: The death did not invalidate the requisition order; the deceased person’s name as a person to be served could be removed, without affecting the order’s enforceability.
issues.legal_principle: An order under section 6(4)(a) was administrative rather than judicial, so the death of a person named in it did not make the order a nullity. Section 13 prescribed modes of service and provided that failure to comply with those requirements did not affect the validity of the order. The deceased person’s name as a person to be served was the only part that needed correction.

predicates.administrative_requisition_order: The challenged order requisitions premises through an administrative process rather than judicial proceedings between named parties.
predicates.person_named_for_service_died_before_ord: A person named as someone to be served with the order died before the order was made.
predicates.order_affects_premises_independently_of_: The order requisitions the premises and its operation does not depend on the deceased person being a party to judicial proceedings.

issues.definition: When an administrative requisition order operates on premises independently of a person named for service, that person’s prior death does not void the order.
